title: Candide, Voltaire
subject: litterature
description: Candide crosses a cruel world still believing that all is for the best. Voltaire demolishes the optimism of Leibniz with relentless irony.

hero.hook: Thirty chapters, corrosive irony, and a closing line that changes everything.

blocks.text: Published in **1759**, **Candide, or Optimism** is the masterpiece of the philosophical tale, a short story that mixes adventure with ideas. **Voltaire**, whose real name was **François-Marie Arouet**, demolishes the idea of a world perfectly ordered by providence, the will of God guiding everything.

In thirty fast chapters, the tale is pure **[[Enlightenment philosophy]]**, the 18th-century movement built on reason and the critique of prejudice. Man must act concretely, not only speculate about the meaning of the world. Voltaire uses humor and exaggeration to make the reader think without preaching.

Voltaire wrote Candide after the **[[Seven Years' War]]**, the great European conflict of 1756 to 1763, and above all after the **Lisbon** earthquake of November 1, **1755**. About 60,000 people died on a religious feast day. How could anyone still believe that every evil serves a higher good?

blocks.caption: The Lisbon earthquake: the disaster that shatters faith in a perfect world

blocks.text: Voltaire attacks **[[Leibnizian optimism]]**. According to that philosophy, God created the best of all possible worlds, and every apparent evil serves a higher good. Candide is born out of that refusal. The philosophical tale mixes light fiction with deep reflection to reach a wide public, not only specialists.

blocks.caption: Voltaire: irony, clear sight and a fight for reason

blocks.text: **Candide**, a naive young man, is raised in the castle of the baron of **Thunder-ten-tronckh** by **Pangloss**, a caricature of **[[Leibniz]]**, the German philosopher of the 17th century. The tutor claims that every event, however dreadful, has a beneficial cause inside a divine plan.
Banned by the Parlement of Paris, the book circulated in secret. More than 20,000 copies are thought to have sold in the first year alone.

Thrown out of the castle for loving **Cunégonde**, the baron's daughter, the hero meets the horrors of the world: forced enlistment in an army, storm, disease and the **[[Inquisition]]**, the church court that hunted heresy. The Inquisition holds an **[[Auto-da-fé]]**, a public ceremony where the condemned are sometimes burned, to prevent further earthquakes.

The absurdity peaks when Pangloss explains that syphilis is indispensable if Europe is to have chocolate. Voltaire pushes the reader to drop abstract speculation and look clearly at the facts. Every disaster becomes a lesson in irony. The tale moves fast, like a run of comic hammer blows aimed at human stupidity.

sections.title: Eldorado and the slave of Surinam

blocks.text: **Eldorado**, an imaginary South American utopia, proves that optimism can hold inside a rational and peaceful society. Yet Candide leaves it to find **Cunégonde** again. Static perfection does not suit human beings: they want to act, to love, to move. Voltaire suggests that happiness is not a state but an activity.
It is at this price that you eat sugar in Europe.

The **slave of Surinam**, mutilated so that Europe can have sugar, pushes Candide to define optimism: “the mania for insisting that all is well when things are going badly.” The tale parodies the novel of education, in which a hero learns life through experience, and forces the reader to look straight at colonial injustice.

The ending takes place on a small Turkish farm, with **Pangloss**, **Cunégonde** and the other companions in misfortune. Candide concludes: “**We must cultivate our garden**.” No more metaphysical speculation about God and the meaning of the world: only concrete action counts. Voltaire refuses every global answer to the evil of the world, but he offers a clear-eyed pragmatism.

blocks.text: **Candide**, published in **1759**, ridicules **[[Leibnizian optimism]]** with irony and concludes that only concrete action, “cultivating our garden,” gives life a meaning.
